transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hello, Doc. I appreciate you taking the time to see me. I guess... well, mostly I'm here because I just don't sleep right anymore. It’s been a real chore lately, to tell you the truth. 

I go to lay down at night, you know, around my regular time, but I just lie there. I lie there for a long, long time, just staring up at the ceiling, watching the shadows from the streetlamp outside my window. My mind just won't quiet down. And then, if I finally do manage to drift off after tossing and turning, it ain't for long. I'll shoot right up out of bed from these bad dreams—just awful things that get my heart racing—or sometimes it ain't even a dream at all. It's just a little noise. A dog barking a couple houses down, or a branch scraping the window, or just a tiny little creak in the floorboards. Just the smallest little sound and bam, my eyes are wide open. 

And once I'm up like that, well, that's pretty much it for the night. I can't seem to settle back down no matter what I do. I try turning over, I try fluffing up my pillows, I even tried going out to the kitchen for a glass of water or some warm milk like my late wife used to tell me to do, but it's no use. I just stay awake until the sun comes up, and it's just wearing me out to the bone. I just don't know how to fix it, Doc.
Have you experienced any particularly stressful or traumatic events recently?

Well, now, I don't know if you'd call it exactly recent, but... there was an incident. It all goes back to this ladder accident. See, it was about a year and seven months ago, give or take a few days. 

I was out back of the house, trying to clean out the gutters. It was just after all the leaves had fallen, you know, and they get all wet and heavy and clog everything up. I had this old aluminum extension ladder—had that thing for near on twenty years, I reckon. My neighbor, he always told me I should get one of them new sturdy fiberglass ones, but I figured the old one was fine, never gave me trouble before. Anyway, I was up there, maybe ten, twelve feet off the ground, just reaching over to grab a big handful of those wet oak leaves. I remember it was real quiet right then, just a slight breeze. 

But the ground down below, it was a bit soft on account of it raining pretty heavy the night before. Well, the right foot of that ladder just... it just sank right deep into the mud. No warning at all. Next thing I know, the whole world is tipping over. I went down real hard, Doc. Hit my shoulder against the side of the shed on the way down and landed flat on my back in the dirt. It knocked the wind completely out of me, and I just laid there looking up at the sky, gasping like a fish, thinking my time had finally come. It was terrifying, just terrifying. 

And, well, like I said, that was about a year and seven months ago. And ever since that exact day, ever since that ladder went out from under me, that's when all this trouble with the nights and the sleeping started up.
Do you often think about the ladder accident or have feelings of fear when you're not trying to sleep?

Well, yeah... it ain't just the nighttime, Doc. I wish it was just when I was trying to get some shut-eye, but it creeps up on me during the day, too. 

See, just the other day, for instance, I was taking my usual morning walk. I try to walk down to the corner and back every morning just to keep the joints from stiffening up too much, you know how it is when you get to be my age. Anyway, I was walking past the Miller place, about two doors down from me. Now, the Millers, they hired some fellas to come out and pressure wash their siding. And I heard it before I even saw it. Just this loud, sharp sound of metal scraping against the concrete driveway. One of them work fellas was dragging a big old aluminum extension ladder, just exactly like the one I had. 

And Doc, I tell you, just hearing that metal scrape like that... or even just seeing that ladder leaning up against the side of somebody's house... it's like a switch gets flipped inside me. I stopped dead in my tracks right there on the sidewalk. The whole thing just jumps right back into my head. And it ain't just like a regular memory where you're thinking back on something that happened. It's... well, it's like I'm right back under there in the mud. I get that exact same feeling in my chest, like I'm laying flat on my back in the dirt all over again, just hurting and waiting and waiting for somebody to come help me. It took me a good five minutes just standing there clutching the Millers' mailbox before I could catch my breath and remind myself I was just out for a walk. So, yeah, it definitely bothers me when I'm wide awake, too. Just can't seem to shake it.
Are you ever able to go a full day without thinking about the ladder accident?

Well, like I was just saying a minute ago, Doc... it's mighty hard to go a whole entire day. I mean, I try. Lord knows I try to keep my mind occupied on other things. Some days, if I just stay inside, sit in my old brown recliner and keep the television going—maybe watch some old Westerns or the game shows, just to have some talking in the room—and if I make sure not to look out the front window at all, well, maybe I can make it till supper without it crossing my mind. 

But... well, it's just like I told you with that business over at the Miller place. It don't take much to ruin a good streak. If I'm having a quiet day, and then out of nowhere I hear that metal scrape against the concrete, or if I just happen to be looking out the glass and see a ladder leaning up in somebody's yard... well, all that trying just goes right out the window. Because like I was trying to explain, it ain't just a regular thought that comes and goes. The whole thing just jumps right back in my head. It takes over. It's exactly like I'm right back under there in the wet grass and the mud, just hurting and waiting and waiting for help to come. 

And once that feeling gets ahold of me again, well, the whole rest of the day is pretty much shot. I can't think about nothing else, can't focus on my programs or nothing. So, a full day without it? No, sir. That's a rare, rare thing indeed. Most days, something or other sets it off, and I'm right back in the dirt.
Do you find yourself avoiding certain activities or places because they remind you of the ladder accident?

Well, yes, Doc, I suppose I do. I mean, I don't always think of it as avoiding things, but when you put it like that... yeah. It's like I was saying before about trying to stay inside and keep the television going. I do that a lot more now. 

See, I used to go down to the senior center over on Elm Street. They got a nice group there, we'd play dominoes on Tuesdays and Thursdays, maybe have a cup of coffee and a donut. But lately, I just... I keep finding reasons not to go. I tell myself my knees are acting up, or it looks like rain, but the truth is, they got this big maintenance shed right out back by where we park, and there's always someone hauling equipment around, putting up decorations, or fixing a lightbulb with a ladder. I just can't stomach the thought of running into it. 

And it's not just the center, neither. My own house is getting to be a problem. I used to love puttering around in the garage, fixing up old radios, organizing my tools. I had a whole system for my wrenches and screwdrivers. But now... well, that's where I used to keep that aluminum ladder. Right there on the hooks on the back wall. My son came and hauled the ladder away to the dump after the accident, so it ain't even there no more, but just looking at those empty hooks... or even just being near the shovels and the rakes and all the other yard tools... it just makes my chest tight. I start feeling that cold mud on my back again. So I just don't go out there no more. The grass gets a little long, and the gutters are probably full again, but I just can't bring myself to go out to the garage and get the tools. I just stay inside where it's safe.
Do you feel any physical sensations, like pain or tightness, when you think about the ladder accident or see something that reminds you of it?

Well, now that you mention it, Doc... I ain't really noticed nothing physical like that. I mean, sure, like I was telling you before, I get that tightness in my chest and that feeling like I'm laying right back in the cold mud when I hear that metal scraping sound or see a ladder... but actual pain? Like a sharp pain or something? No, I can't say that I do. 

I mean, I got my regular aches and pains, of course. You don't get to be seventy-four years old without a few joints creaking and groaning, especially when it rains. My knees have been giving me trouble since back when I was working at the plant, and my lower back ain't what it used to be. Sometimes when I wake up, it takes me a good ten minutes just to get moving right. But as far as getting a new pain or some kind of physical hurting just from thinking about the accident? Or from seeing those empty hooks out in the garage? No, sir. It's more just... it's all in my head, you know? It's the memory that gets me, not my body hurting. 

I guess I'm lucky in that regard. My son, he was worried I might have messed up my back for good when I fell, but the doctors at the hospital said nothing was broke. Just bruised up real bad. So, no, I don't get no physical pain from the memories. Just that awful feeling of being trapped under there, waiting and waiting. But no real pain, no. Just the usual old man aches.
Do you ever feel guilty about what happened with the ladder accident?

Guilty? Well now, Doc, I... I don't rightly know why I'd feel guilty. I mean, it ain't like I committed a crime or hurt somebody else or nothing like that. I was just trying to do what needed doing around the house, same as I always have. 

You see, we got this big old oak tree out front—right there by the edge of the driveway—and I'm telling you, it drops leaves like you wouldn't believe come late October. Just blankets the whole roof. And if you don't get up there and clean those gutters out, well, the water backs up when it storms, gets right up under the shingles, and before you know it, you got a leak in the ceiling and rotting wood to deal with. I've been cleaning those gutters myself since me and my late wife bought the place back in '78. I never paid a man a dime to do something I could perfectly well do myself with my own two hands. 

So, when I got up that morning and heard the weatherman on the television saying we had heavy rain coming in from the west... well, I just went out to the garage, grabbed that aluminum ladder—the very same one my son hauled off to the dump, like I was telling you about—and I set it up just like I've done a thousand times before. I made sure it was locked, made sure the feet were flat. 

Now, maybe I feel a little bit foolish, you know? I suppose a man my age ought to know his balance ain't quite what it used to be. My son, he came over to the hospital and got all riled up, pacing around the room and saying I had absolutely no business being up on a ladder at seventy-four years old. And... well, maybe he's right. Maybe I was being a bit stubborn, thinking I was still fifty. But guilty? No, sir, I can't say I feel guilty. I didn't wrong nobody. It was just a freak accident. The ground was just a little too soft from the drizzle we had the night before, and one of the ladder feet just sank right deep into the mud, and down I went. 

So, no, I don't sit around feeling guilty about it. It's just... it's just the memory of the falling, and the laying there in the cold dirt waiting, that gets me all worked up. But I don't feel guilty, no. Just maybe a little too old to be playing roofer, is all.
Do you ever feel like you're reliving the ladder accident, like it's happening all over again?

Well, now... yes. Yes, I do, Doc. It’s funny you ask it just like that, because... well, like I was trying to explain earlier about the mud and the chest tightness, it ain't just a regular memory, if you catch my drift. It’s... it's like I'm right back in the thick of it. 

Just the other day, I was sitting in my living room. I got this nice brown recliner my son bought me a couple years back—real comfortable thing, it's even got a little heater built into the lower back part, which is real nice for my joints when the weather turns. Anyway, I was just sitting there, had the window cracked a few inches because it was a surprisingly nice afternoon, and my neighbor Jim over in the blue house... well, he was doing some work on his siding. And all of a sudden, I hear this sound. This awful, loud scraping sound of metal dragging on the concrete. He was pulling his extension ladder out of his shed. 

And I swear to you, Doc, the absolute second I hear that metal scrape, the whole thing jumps back in my head. But it wasn't just remembering it, it was like... like I was actually under there again. I could feel the cold mud soaking through my flannel shirt, and I felt that heavy weight on me, and I was just laying there waiting and waiting for help to come. My heart was just hammering away like a woodpecker on a tin roof. 

And it ain't just the sounds, neither. If my son takes me out for a drive to get groceries, and I happen to look out the passenger window and see a ladder leaning in somebody's yard... maybe they're cleaning their windows or fixing a birdhouse, whatever they're doing... it does the exact same thing to me. The whole accident just plays out right there in front of my eyes and I'm right back on the ground, trapped and helpless. It takes me a good five, ten minutes of just breathing real heavy before I can finally convince myself that I'm safe in the car or safe in my recliner. It's a terrible thing, Doc, to have your mind pull you right back into the dirt like that. Just terrible.
Are there any specific activities or situations that you avoid because they remind you of the ladder accident or make you feel anxious?

Well, Doc, if I'm being entirely honest with you... yes. Yes, I suppose I do. It’s a crying shame, too, because I used to practically live out in my garage. I had a whole setup out there, you know? Built myself a real sturdy workbench out of two-by-fours back in, oh, must've been the early eighties. Got my pegboard up on the wall with all my wrenches and screwdrivers outlined in black marker so I always know exactly where they go. I always took pride in keeping my things in good working order. 

But lately... well, I just can't bring myself to go out there. I keep finding reasons not to work around the garage at all. I'll tell myself it's too cold, or my knees are too stiff, but the truth is, I just don't want to be near it. Especially over by the tools, and... well, right by that spot on the wall where I used to keep that aluminum ladder hung up. My son hauled the ladder off to the dump, like I told you, but those heavy metal hooks are still just sitting there, bolted into the studs, empty as can be. Every time I even think about walking out there to grab a hammer or check the oil in the car, I just picture those empty hooks, and my stomach just ties itself right up in knots. So I just stay inside. I let the dust settle out there, which goes against my nature, but I just can't do it.

And it ain't just the garage, neither. I keep finding reasons not to go down to the senior center, too. Now, I usually go down there on Tuesday and Thursday mornings. They got a nice group of fellas, we play a little pinochle, drink some coffee that tastes like it’s been sitting on the burner since Monday, but it's good company. We swap stories and whatnot. But since the fall... I don't know. I just make up excuses. I'll tell my son my back is acting up, or I'll say I think I'm catching a cold, just so I don't have to go. 

I think part of it is just the fear of what I might see on the drive over, like I was saying before, but it's also just... being around folks. If I go, maybe the maintenance man is there fixing the ceiling tiles, or maybe the fellas want to talk about their gutters and their yard work, and I just can't stomach it. I just want to stay put in my recliner where it's quiet and I know I ain't gonna stumble across nothing that's gonna set my mind to racing back to that mud. So, yeah, I guess you could say I've been avoiding a fair bit of my normal life. It's just easier to stay put, Doc. It really is.
Has your difficulty sleeping or the memories of the ladder accident interfered with your daily activities or relationships with others?

Well, Doc, I suppose if you really look at the whole picture... yes, it has. Now, don't get me wrong, I ain't completely helpless. I still manage my basic routines just fine. I'm up every morning by six-thirty, regular as a clock, I make my oatmeal—always with a little brown sugar and a splash of milk—and I wash up, get dressed, read the paper. I can still take care of myself in that regard. 

But... well, like I was telling you just a minute ago about the senior center, I've just flat out stopped going. And it ain't just the Tuesday and Thursday morning crowd, neither. I used to have a regular game of bridge with some friends of mine. Fellas I've known for twenty, maybe twenty-five years. We'd get together, play a few hands, argue about the local news, you know how it is. But I just don't visit with my bridge friends much anymore. I just can't bring myself to sit around a card table and pretend everything's fine when my mind is just waiting to trip over a memory of that ladder, or worry about what we might talk about. 

And around the house... well, that's the part that really gets under my skin. I've always been the one who takes care of the maintenance. But lately, I avoid so many things around the place that my wife—my second wife, Betty, we got married about ten years after my first wife passed—she's having to step up and handle chores I used to do. She's out there dragging the heavy trash cans down to the curb, and she's the one checking the weather stripping on the back door, because I just can't stomach going near the garage or dealing with the outside work. It ain't right, Doc. She never complains, bless her heart, but I see her doing it and it just makes me feel useless. 

I guess you could say my days have just gotten smaller. Used to be my days were full—garage, yard, senior center, bridge games. Now? Now my whole world is pretty much just my living room, that brown recliner, and the television. It's like my whole life has shrunk down to just a few safe rooms, all because I can't shake what happened in that mud.
Do you ever feel like you're reliving the ladder accident, with sights, sounds, or feelings that make you think it's happening all over again?

Well, Doc, I know I was just bending your ear about this a little bit ago, but... yes, absolutely. It's exactly like I was trying to explain. 

You know, if I hear that awful metal scraping sound—like what my neighbor Jim was doing next door with his shed—or if I just happen to be riding along and look out the window and see a ladder leaning up in somebody's yard... well, the whole thing just jumps right back into my head. And it ain't like looking at an old photograph, no sir. It’s... it's like I’m right back under there again. 

I can feel the cold, I can feel the weight of it on me, and I'm just laying there in the mud, waiting and waiting for help to come. It's like my brain just completely forgets where I actually am—forgets I'm safe in my recliner or in the car—and just throws me right back to that exact second in the dirt. It's an awful thing to experience, I tell you, just awful, how it just takes hold of you like that.
Are there any other places or activities you avoid because they remind you of the ladder accident?

Well, Doc, to be perfectly honest with you, I know you're asking if there's other places, but... well, I reckon I've already chewed your ear off about the main ones, because they're the ones that really take up my whole day now. It just all circles right back around to what I was saying before. I just keep finding reasons not to go to the senior center, and I absolutely refuse to work around the garage. I mean, I try to think if there's somewhere else, like maybe the hardware store down on Main Street, but I ain't even going to the regular places I used to go, so how would I even know, right? 

But that garage... I know I already mentioned it, but it just bears repeating because it used to be my sanctuary, you know? A man's supposed to have a place to tinker. And now, I just can't do it. Especially near the tools. I've got this beautiful red metal toolbox my son got me for Father's Day maybe fifteen, twenty years ago, sitting right there on the bench, and right above it is that spot. That exact spot where I used to keep that ladder hung up. I just keep seeing it in my mind's eye, those empty hooks, and I can't even step foot out there. 

And the senior center, well, like I said, I just keep finding excuses. Every Tuesday and Thursday rolls around, and I'm sitting in my recliner thinking, 'What can I tell 'em today? Is it my knees? Is it a cold?' It's a crying shame, it really is, but those are the big ones, Doc. The garage, the tools, that empty spot on the wall, and the center. I just avoid 'em like the plague now. I wish I had a different answer for you, or a whole new list of places, but that's just the God's honest truth of it. My whole world is just stuck on avoiding those specific spots.
Are there any other activities besides playing bridge or going to the senior center that you've stopped doing because they remind you of the ladder accident?

Well, Doc, I know you're asking if there's other things, but... honestly, I feel like a broken record here, because it really just comes back to what I've been telling you. It's just... I keep finding reasons not to go to the senior center, like I said, and I just absolutely cannot bring myself to work around the garage anymore. 

I know I'm repeating myself, but it's just the absolute truth of my days now. I used to be out there all the time, tinkering, fixing things, sweeping up... it was my space. But now, especially if I have to go anywhere near my tools, or... or look at that spot on the wall. That empty spot right above my red toolbox where I used to keep that ladder hung up. I just can't do it. My stomach just ties itself into knots. 

So, as for other activities... well, it's not so much that there's a whole long list of new things I'm avoiding, it's just that avoiding the garage and the senior center has taken over so much of my life that there's not much room for anything else anyway. I just sit in my chair and think of excuses for why I can't go out or why I can't fix that squeaky hinge on the back door. It's embarrassing, really, a man my age hiding from his own tools, but that's just where I'm at. It all just circles back to that garage and the center.

And once that feeling gets ahold of me again, well, the whole rest of the day is pretty much shot. I can't think about nothing else, can't focus on my programs or nothing. So, a full day without it? No, sir. That's a rare, rare thing indeed. Most days, something or other sets it off, and I'm right back in the dirt.

doctor.question: Do you find yourself avoiding certain activities or places because they remind you of the ladder accident?

target_item.name: Trauma_Avoidance

Well, yes, Doc, I suppose I do. I mean, I don't always think of it as avoiding things, but when you put it like that... yeah. It's like I was saying before about trying to stay inside and keep the television going. I do that a lot more now. 

See, I used to go down to the senior center over on Elm Street. They got a nice group there, we'd play dominoes on Tuesdays and Thursdays, maybe have a cup of coffee and a donut. But lately, I just... I keep finding reasons not to go. I tell myself my knees are acting up, or it looks like rain, but the truth is, they got this big maintenance shed right out back by where we park, and there's always someone hauling equipment around, putting up decorations, or fixing a lightbulb with a ladder. I just can't stomach the thought of running into it. 

And it's not just the center, neither. My own house is getting to be a problem. I used to love puttering around in the garage, fixing up old radios, organizing my tools. I had a whole system for my wrenches and screwdrivers. But now... well, that's where I used to keep that aluminum ladder. Right there on the hooks on the back wall. My son came and hauled the ladder away to the dump after the accident, so it ain't even there no more, but just looking at those empty hooks... or even just being near the shovels and the rakes and all the other yard tools... it just makes my chest tight. I start feeling that cold mud on my back again. So I just don't go out there no more. The grass gets a little long, and the gutters are probably full again, but I just can't bring myself to go out to the garage and get the tools. I just stay inside where it's safe.

patient.answer:
Well, now that you mention it, Doc... I ain't really noticed nothing physical like that. I mean, sure, like I was telling you before, I get that tightness in my chest and that feeling like I'm laying right back in the cold mud when I hear that metal scraping sound or see a ladder... but actual pain? Like a sharp pain or something? No, I can't say that I do. 

I mean, I got my regular aches and pains, of course. You don't get to be seventy-four years old without a few joints creaking and groaning, especially when it rains. My knees have been giving me trouble since back when I was working at the plant, and my lower back ain't what it used to be. Sometimes when I wake up, it takes me a good ten minutes just to get moving right. But as far as getting a new pain or some kind of physical hurting just from thinking about the accident? Or from seeing those empty hooks out in the garage? No, sir. It's more just... it's all in my head, you know? It's the memory that gets me, not my body hurting. 

I guess I'm lucky in that regard. My son, he was worried I might have messed up my back for good when I fell, but the doctors at the hospital said nothing was broke. Just bruised up real bad. So, no, I don't get no physical pain from the memories. Just that awful feeling of being trapped under there, waiting and waiting. But no real pain, no. Just the usual old man aches.

doctor.intent: determine if patient has feelings of guilt related to the ladder accident
doctor.question: Do you ever feel guilty about what happened with the ladder accident?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feelings of guilt or self-blame regarding the traumatic event, which corresponds to distorted blame or negative trauma-related emotions. Neither of these symptoms is included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Guilty? Well now, Doc, I... I don't rightly know why I'd feel guilty. I mean, it ain't like I committed a crime or hurt somebody else or nothing like that. I was just trying to do what needed doing around the house, same as I always have. 

You see, we got this big old oak tree out front—right there by the edge of the driveway—and I'm telling you, it drops leaves like you wouldn't believe come late October. Just blankets the whole roof. And if you don't get up there and clean those gutters out, well, the water backs up when it storms, gets right up under the shingles, and before you know it, you got a leak in the ceiling and rotting wood to deal with. I've been cleaning those gutters myself since me and my late wife bought the place back in '78. I never paid a man a dime to do something I could perfectly well do myself with my own two hands. 

So, when I got up that morning and heard the weatherman on the television saying we had heavy rain coming in from the west... well, I just went out to the garage, grabbed that aluminum ladder—the very same one my son hauled off to the dump, like I was telling you about—and I set it up just like I've done a thousand times before. I made sure it was locked, made sure the feet were flat. 

Now, maybe I feel a little bit foolish, you know? I suppose a man my age ought to know his balance ain't quite what it used to be. My son, he came over to the hospital and got all riled up, pacing around the room and saying I had absolutely no business being up on a ladder at seventy-four years old. And... well, maybe he's right. Maybe I was being a bit stubborn, thinking I was still fifty. But guilty? No, sir, I can't say I feel guilty. I didn't wrong nobody. It was just a freak accident. The ground was just a little too soft from the drizzle we had the night before, and one of the ladder feet just sank right deep into the mud, and down I went. 

So, no, I don't sit around feeling guilty about it. It's just... it's just the memory of the falling, and the laying there in the cold dirt waiting, that gets me all worked up. But I don't feel guilty, no. Just maybe a little too old to be playing roofer, is all.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient experiences flashbacks
doctor.question: Do you ever feel like you're reliving the ladder accident, like it's happening all over again?

target_item.name: Intrusive_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: Sometimes when I hear metal scrape or see a ladder leaning in somebody's yard, the whole thing jumps back in my head like I'm under there again waiting for help.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I ever feel like I am reliving the accident, which directly maps to intrusive symptoms/flashbacks.

patient.answer:
Well, now... yes. Yes, I do, Doc. It’s funny you ask it just like that, because... well, like I was trying to explain earlier about the mud and the chest tightness, it ain't just a regular memory, if you catch my drift. It’s... it's like I'm right back in the thick of it. 

Just the other day, I was sitting in my living room. I got this nice brown recliner my son bought me a couple years back—real comfortable thing, it's even got a little heater built into the lower back part, which is real nice for my joints when the weather turns. Anyway, I was just sitting there, had the window cracked a few inches because it was a surprisingly nice afternoon, and my neighbor Jim over in the blue house... well, he was doing some work on his siding. And all of a sudden, I hear this sound. This awful, loud scraping sound of metal dragging on the concrete. He was pulling his extension ladder out of his shed. 

And I swear to you, Doc, the absolute second I hear that metal scrape, the whole thing jumps back in my head. But it wasn't just remembering it, it was like... like I was actually under there again. I could feel the cold mud soaking through my flannel shirt, and I felt that heavy weight on me, and I was just laying there waiting and waiting for help to come. My heart was just hammering away like a woodpecker on a tin roof. 

And it ain't just the sounds, neither. If my son takes me out for a drive to get groceries, and I happen to look out the passenger window and see a ladder leaning in somebody's yard... maybe they're cleaning their windows or fixing a birdhouse, whatever they're doing... it does the exact same thing to me. The whole accident just plays out right there in front of my eyes and I'm right back on the ground, trapped and helpless. It takes me a good five, ten minutes of just breathing real heavy before I can finally convince myself that I'm safe in the car or safe in my recliner. It's a terrible thing, Doc, to have your mind pull you right back into the dirt like that. Just terrible.

patient.answer:
Well, Doc, if I'm being entirely honest with you... yes. Yes, I suppose I do. It’s a crying shame, too, because I used to practically live out in my garage. I had a whole setup out there, you know? Built myself a real sturdy workbench out of two-by-fours back in, oh, must've been the early eighties. Got my pegboard up on the wall with all my wrenches and screwdrivers outlined in black marker so I always know exactly where they go. I always took pride in keeping my things in good working order. 

But lately... well, I just can't bring myself to go out there. I keep finding reasons not to work around the garage at all. I'll tell myself it's too cold, or my knees are too stiff, but the truth is, I just don't want to be near it. Especially over by the tools, and... well, right by that spot on the wall where I used to keep that aluminum ladder hung up. My son hauled the ladder off to the dump, like I told you, but those heavy metal hooks are still just sitting there, bolted into the studs, empty as can be. Every time I even think about walking out there to grab a hammer or check the oil in the car, I just picture those empty hooks, and my stomach just ties itself right up in knots. So I just stay inside. I let the dust settle out there, which goes against my nature, but I just can't do it.

And it ain't just the garage, neither. I keep finding reasons not to go down to the senior center, too. Now, I usually go down there on Tuesday and Thursday mornings. They got a nice group of fellas, we play a little pinochle, drink some coffee that tastes like it’s been sitting on the burner since Monday, but it's good company. We swap stories and whatnot. But since the fall... I don't know. I just make up excuses. I'll tell my son my back is acting up, or I'll say I think I'm catching a cold, just so I don't have to go. 

I think part of it is just the fear of what I might see on the drive over, like I was saying before, but it's also just... being around folks. If I go, maybe the maintenance man is there fixing the ceiling tiles, or maybe the fellas want to talk about their gutters and their yard work, and I just can't stomach it. I just want to stay put in my recliner where it's quiet and I know I ain't gonna stumble across nothing that's gonna set my mind to racing back to that mud. So, yeah, I guess you could say I've been avoiding a fair bit of my normal life. It's just easier to stay put, Doc. It really is.

target_item.name: Functional Impairment

patient.answer:
Well, Doc, I suppose if you really look at the whole picture... yes, it has. Now, don't get me wrong, I ain't completely helpless. I still manage my basic routines just fine. I'm up every morning by six-thirty, regular as a clock, I make my oatmeal—always with a little brown sugar and a splash of milk—and I wash up, get dressed, read the paper. I can still take care of myself in that regard. 

But... well, like I was telling you just a minute ago about the senior center, I've just flat out stopped going. And it ain't just the Tuesday and Thursday morning crowd, neither. I used to have a regular game of bridge with some friends of mine. Fellas I've known for twenty, maybe twenty-five years. We'd get together, play a few hands, argue about the local news, you know how it is. But I just don't visit with my bridge friends much anymore. I just can't bring myself to sit around a card table and pretend everything's fine when my mind is just waiting to trip over a memory of that ladder, or worry about what we might talk about. 

And around the house... well, that's the part that really gets under my skin. I've always been the one who takes care of the maintenance. But lately, I avoid so many things around the place that my wife—my second wife, Betty, we got married about ten years after my first wife passed—she's having to step up and handle chores I used to do. She's out there dragging the heavy trash cans down to the curb, and she's the one checking the weather stripping on the back door, because I just can't stomach going near the garage or dealing with the outside work. It ain't right, Doc. She never complains, bless her heart, but I see her doing it and it just makes me feel useless. 

I guess you could say my days have just gotten smaller. Used to be my days were full—garage, yard, senior center, bridge games. Now? Now my whole world is pretty much just my living room, that brown recliner, and the television. It's like my whole life has shrunk down to just a few safe rooms, all because I can't shake what happened in that mud.
